title: Biblical Commentary on the Books of Samuel
author: Carl Friedrich Keil; Franz Delitzsch (trans. James Martin)
allowedUseNotes: Public-domain 19th-century commentary (original German editions 1864-1875; this English translation published 1866, pre-1928). May be cited, quoted in short excerpt, or paraphrased freely with attribution; no full-chapter reproduction needed per this project's own tighter internal policy regardless.
summary: Classic 19th-century verse-by-verse critical-conservative commentary on 1-2 Samuel, part of the larger multi-volume Keil-Delitzsch Commentary on the Old Testament (the Samuel volume's exegetical work is Keil's; Delitzsch is credited on the original title page as the series' co-author/editor). On 1 Samuel 31:12-13, Keil explains the men of Jabesh-gilead's burning of Saul's and his sons' bodies as arising from the specific circumstances rather than ordinary Israelite funerary custom: the bodies had already been mutilated (decapitated) and displayed on Beth-shan's wall, making a normal burial impossible in the usual sense, and the men of Jabesh feared further desecration if the Philistines followed up their victory and reached Jabesh. Keil also reports and rejects an older Targumic/rabbinic reading (also discussed in the Gill source card) that the 'burning' refers to ceremonial burning of spices over the bodies rather than cremation of the flesh itself, arguing the Hebrew phrasing here differs from the idiom used for that funerary-spice custom elsewhere (e.g., the 'very great burning' made for King Asa, 2 Chronicles 16:14). On 2 Samuel 1:1-10, Keil addresses the Amalekite messenger's claim to have killed Saul at the king's own request, directly against 1 Samuel 31:3-5's own narration of Saul falling on his own sword unaided. Keil's reading: the only part of the messenger's account that can be taken as certainly true is that he came upon Saul already lying dead on the field and stripped the crown from his head and the armlet from his arm; the claim to have delivered the death-blow himself is judged an invented embellishment, told to secure a reward and a welcome from the new king. Keil also notes the narrative gives no way to determine whether the Amalekite's arrival at Ziklag preceded or followed David's own return from pursuing the Amalekite raiders (1 Samuel 30), only that the two are narrated as close in time. Coverage extended (2026-08-11, queue #20a) to 2 Samuel 3 and 4. On 2 Samuel 3:7-8, Keil reads Ish-bosheth's accusation that Abner had gone in to Rizpah, Saul's concubine, against its wider ancient Near Eastern political background: 'it was the exclusive right of the successor to the throne to cohabit with the concubine of the deceased king, who came down to him as part of the property which he inherited' (per this custom rather than Mosaic law) — i.e., Ish-bosheth's accusation, true or not, amounted to reading Abner's act as a bid for the throne itself. On 2 Samuel 4:6, a verse widely flagged as textually difficult, Keil reads the Masoretic Hebrew (Rechab and Baanah entering the house 'as though to fetch wheat') as the base text, and explains the Septuagint's fuller reading (a female doorkeeper sifting/cleaning wheat who grew drowsy and fell asleep, letting the two men slip past her) as the Greek translator's own explanatory paraphrase, added to account for how the killers gained entry — i.e., Keil treats the LXX's doorkeeper detail as secondary elaboration on the same underlying text rather than an independently more original account.
